newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-New York tosses tickertape parade for Yankees.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-New York tosses tickertape parade for Yankees.

text.p: New York City paid its champion baseball team the New York Yankees its highest honour on Tuesday, throwing a jubilant tickertape parade through the towering skyscrapers of downtown Manhattan.
A crowd calculated officially at three-and-a-half million people jammed sidewalks and sidestreets, standing 40 deep and roaring with delight as the Yankees passed by.

The winners of baseball's World Series for the first time in 18 years, the Yankees rode in a caravan of floats up the city's so-called Canyon of Heroes, a cavernous stretch of lower Broadway lined by office towers.

The unique New York tradition of tickertape parades began spontaneously 110 years ago, when workers threw paper tape out windows for the dedication of the Statue of Liberty. Since then, such heroes as Charles Lindbergh, Gen. Douglas MacArthur and the first astronauts on the moon have been so honoured.
While the era of tickertape has long since given way to the computer age, there was no shortage of confetti and streamers for Tuesday's parade.
The shredded paper, which office workers tossed out windows by the armful, sparkled like snow in the sun as it floated to the streets below.
Parents hoisted children onto their shoulders, men in expensive suits clambered on top telephone booths to get a glimpse of the parading champions.
Even New Yorkers who didn't plan to take part in the celebration had little choice, as revellers filled the city's subway trains and brought traffic on many streets to a halt.

Along the parade route, the biggest cheers erupted over outfielder Darryl Strawberry, who battled drug abuse and legal problems and spent a stint back on a minor league team before donning the Yankee's trademark pinstripe uniform this season.

Another big crowdpleaser was Yankee manager and New York City native Joe Torre, all smiles as he waved to the happy mob. Torre's intensely glum face became a familiar sight to baseball fans as he sat in the dugout guiding the team to the come-from-behind victory over the Atlanta Braves.
For the 56-year-old Torre, whose down-to-earth style made him perhaps the most memorable character of the Series, it was his first trip ever to the championship after a long career.

"I was wondering why it took so long for me to get to a World Series, 4,200-plus games, 30-plus years," he told the crowd at City Hall. "I guess the good Lord was waiting for me to put on the pinstripes."
The Yankees won the championship series on Saturday, defeating the Braves four games to two.

Even Yankee owner George Steinbrenner was cheered by fans, who usually revile him for tempestuously firing managers or more recently threatening to move the team out of its stadium in the city's Bronx borough to Manhattan or nearby New Jersey.
"Going to Yankee stadium is like going to church," explained Kevin Fitzpatrick, a city busdriver and Yankee fan. "It's something special."
The crowd agreed, chanting "Keep 'em in New York" as Steinbrenner went by.
The parade ended at City Hall, where each Yankee team member was presented with a key to the city.

Earlier, Wall Street honoured Torre when he rang the opening bell at the New York Stock Exchange. "It was a warm moment," said Art Cashin, a floor broker at PaineWebber. "When it came to ringing the bell, Joe Torre scored a clear run."
The most recent tickertape parade was held in 1994 for the New York Rangers hockey team which won the Stanley Cup.

Tuesday's parade, which involved thousands of police officers and clean-up crews, was estimated to cost $1 million. City officials said they they expected the cost to be covered by corporate sponsors that paid for signs along the parade route.
